speaker: Drago Anguelov
title: Inside Waymo's New Foundation Model Powering Self-Driving Cars [Drago Anguelov]
question: In autonomous driving, why does scaling safety validation not work the same way as scaling model training with more data?
guest: Validation is extremely hard. As you collect more data and make your model larger, you can have it predict better trajectories. If you just want the driver to improve over time, you can keep adding more and better data suitably picked, and the model will improve in general. When you want to test it, you cannot do that. You actually need to think about all the cases that could go wrong and create ways to validate all of them—hardware failures, sensors going wrong, rare edge cases, you name it—and handle all of this in your release cycle. It does not work to just take more data and feed it into the simulator and expect the simulator to test you better. It's not purely a data-driven exercise. You need experts thinking about what could go wrong and working on mitigating that. Your ability to test the system simply does not scale as straightforwardly as putting more data in to improve the driver.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Training and validation ask fundamentally different things of data. Training improves average performance: each additional mile or clip nudges the model toward better behavior on the common distribution, and returns diminish gracefully. Validation instead has to prove the absence of rare, catastrophic failures, and that is a statistical problem dominated by the long tail.

Because human drivers have a fatal crash only about once per 100 million miles, demonstrating with confidence that a system is as safe or safer requires hundreds of millions to billions of test miles (the well-known RAND estimate), and every software update can in principle invalidate that evidence, forcing re-validation. More data of the usual kind barely helps, since the dangerous cases are rare, diverse, and often unknown in advance; you cannot sample your way to confidence about events you almost never see.

Validation also needs independence and realism: testing on data resembling the training set overstates safety, and simulation only counts if its fidelity is itself validated. So safety cases rely on structured arguments, scenario-based testing, rare-event simulation, and redundancy, not just more miles.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Model training scales with data because neural networks extract generalizable patterns from routine driving, and historical logs remain reusable across architecture or weight updates. Safety validation, however, must bound the probability of catastrophic failures—events so rare in the long tail of traffic that statistically proving human-level safety requires billions of miles of real-world exposure. Worse, whereas training datasets accumulate over time, empirical safety evidence resets whenever the system changes: even a minor model update can introduce novel failure modes, invalidating prior mileage guarantees and requiring fresh verification. Replaying recorded logs offline cannot solve this because driving is a closed-loop, interactive process; once an updated policy deviates slightly from the logged trajectory, surrounding road users would respond differently, rendering static data counterfactual and unreliable for measuring true crash risk. While simulation offers synthetic closed-loop scale, its safety guarantees are limited by sim-to-real gaps precisely in rare, safety-critical edge cases, shifting the bottleneck to validating the simulator itself. Consequently, scaling data steadily improves average driving capability without proportionally certifying worst-case safety.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Training and validation answer different questions. Training only needs data to improve average behavior, so every extra mile helps a bit, even if most of it is routine driving. Validation has to show that dangerous failures are extremely rare, and rare events don't scale with ordinary data collection.

Human drivers have roughly one fatal crash per 100 million miles. RAND's 2016 analysis estimated that showing an AV merely matches that rate with statistical confidence takes hundreds of millions of failure-free miles. Showing it is meaningfully better could take billions. The risk sits in a long tail of strange situations that normal driving almost never hits, so piling up more uneventful miles adds very little evidence.

Several things make it worse. Each software update can invalidate earlier results, so the testing has to be redone. Logged data can't show how other road users would have reacted if the car had done something different. Simulation can help, but then the simulator itself has to be proven accurate. Finally, not seeing failures doesn't prove you've covered the situations nobody has thought of yet.

So validation leans on scenario-based testing, targeted searches for rare edge cases, formal safety arguments and staged deployment, rather than just more miles.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
More training data can improve an autonomous driving model by giving it more examples to learn from. Safety validation has a different job. It must establish how often a particular system fails and under what conditions, including rare situations where a mistake can be severe.

A million extra miles on clear, familiar roads can tighten the estimate of failure rates on those roads while adding little evidence about a pedestrian emerging from behind a truck at dusk. Driving is also interactive. A recorded scene shows what happened under the actions actually taken. If the system brakes earlier or chooses a different lane, other road users may react differently.

That’s why validation needs a mix of representative driving to estimate real-world failure rates and targeted, interactive tests to probe rare hazards. The strength of the safety claim depends on which conditions the tests cover, how faithfully they reproduce those conditions, and how much uncertainty remains.
